result:
Solution 3 is the only one whose derivation holds up, so I choose it. I checked its argument but did not verify independently that every layer shares the same parabolic curvature.

**Gibbs integration by parts.** Condition on all curves except 𝓗_n on an interval [a,b]. The curve is then a Brownian bridge reweighted by e^{-∫U ds}, with U(s,ω) = e^{ω-𝓗_{n-1}(s)} + e^{𝓗_{n+1}(s)-ω}. Gaussian integration by parts against a test function φ supported in (a,b) gives E[∫U'φ ds] = -E[∫φ' d𝓗_n].

Taking full expectations and writing g_n = E[𝓗_n], the right side equals ∫φ g_n''. At the point 𝓗_n, U' = e^{𝓗_n-𝓗_{n-1}} - e^{𝓗_{n+1}-𝓗_n}. With A_n = E[e^{𝓗_{n+1}-𝓗_n}], this gives A_1 = -g_1'' and A_{n-1} - A_n = g_n'' for n ≥ 2. I checked the sign for n = 1: the weight favors larger 𝓗_1, and the relation is consistent with a concave mean.

**Curvature of the mean.** The top curve is 𝓗_1 = log Z for the narrow-wedge stochastic heat equation. Under the shear Z(t,x+vt)e^{vx+v²t/2}, the equation and the initial data are preserved, so E[𝓗_1(x)] = c(t) - x²/(2t) and g_1'' = -1/t. Solution 3 claims the same boost acts identically on every layer, so g_k'' = -1/t for all k. I accepted this claim as plausible without verifying it.

**Recursion.** A_1 = 1/t and A_n - A_{n-1} = -g_n'' = 1/t, so A_n = n/t. This is independent of x and decays as t → ∞, as expected.

**The other solutions.** Solution 1 asserts a "conservation law" with no derivation and gets 1. Solution 2 asserts a "Ward-type identity" with no derivation and gets 1/2. Both answers also fail the n = 1 check, which gives 1/t. Neither depends on n or t, and neither is justified.

CHOICE: 3
